title: Ang 1410–1426: saloks beyond the Vars
tomorrow: everything passes, says the ninth Guru. so what stays?

cards: Every app asks how much you're in: a free trial, a monthly plan, or all in. Guru Nanak puts love that way, on ang 1412. In paraphrase: if you want to play the game of love, come to my lane with your head on your palm.
Once you set foot on this road, give your head, and don't make a fuss. That's the price from yesterday's question. So what does love ask of a person?

teach.b: These are the saloks beyond the Vars: short verses of the Gurus that weren't placed inside the ballads, gathered on their own near the end of the Granth. Guru Nanak's answer here is: everything.
Not a donation, not a free weekend. The head is the self, the ego, the thing a person guards first, and love's lane asks for it up front, carried in your own hand.

teach.h: THE HEAD: THE SELF, HANDED OVER.
teach.b: Sikhs read it in stories of courage, and in ordinary days too, the self handed over a little at a time. This question isn't only Sikh.
In the Hebrew Bible, Deuteronomy says: “thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.” Jews say these words in the Shema.
What's shared: love of God that holds nothing back. Not part, not most. All.
And one honest difference. In Deuteronomy it's a commandment, given in a covenant to a people, and the text goes on to say these words are to be taught to children and written on doorposts.
Guru Nanak puts it as an invitation: if you want to play.
Two old voices, two different settings, and the same size of love.

how: Sikhs quote Guru Nanak's 'come to my lane with your head on your palm' in talks and kirtan, and remember it alongside the stories of the Gurus and Sikhs who gave everything.

s: the head-on-palm line is only about dying in battle
Sikhs also read it in ordinary days: the self handed over a little at a time.
Deuteronomy asks for love with all the heart, soul and might
the same size of love Guru Nanak asks for: all of it.
Guru Nanak's line is given as a command
he puts it as an invitation: if you want to play the game of love.

games.q: a classmate reads both lines and says, 'so Sikhs and Jews believe the same thing.' what's the fair reply?
o: both ask for love that holds nothing back; Deuteronomy commands it in a covenant, Guru Nanak invites.
yes, it's the identical teaching, and the names of God are the only difference.
no, they share nothing at all; one is a law code and the other is a poem.
games.why: something shared, honestly told: love with nothing held back. something different, honestly told: a covenant's command, and an invitation to a game. neither is ranked.

practice: Rest one hand open in your lap, palm up, as if it were carrying something. Keep it there through the sit, open, not gripping. Guru Nanak's picture is a head carried on a palm: everything offered, nothing held back.
